concept: An undirected graph's edges go both ways by definition: if A connects to B, B also connects to A.
In code, this means adding an edge requires updating the adjacency structure symmetrically, in both directions, in one operation.

That symmetry is easy to forget in practice — insert only A→B and the graph silently behaves like a directed one from B's side, which is a common source of subtle graph bugs that only show up when traversal starts from the 'wrong' end.
1.analogy: A two-way street, or a friendship — if A is friends with B, B is necessarily friends with A too. There's no version of this connection that only runs one way.
1.mascotDialogue: One edge, two entries in the adjacency matrix. Forget the second one, and you've quietly built half a directed graph instead.

2.mascotDialogue: Line 2 and line 3 are not optional extras of each other — they're the same conceptual edge, and they must be added as a single atomic pair, every time.

3.mascotDialogue: No arrowheads this time — just a plain line, because the connection is inherently mutual.

4.bugDescription: The function is named addUndirectedEdge but only wrote adjacency[u][v]. The result is functionally a directed edge masquerading as undirected — traversal from vertex 1 will never reach vertex 0 through this connection, even though the graph is meant to treat them as mutually connected.
4.mascotDialogue: The visual shows a single arrowhead where an undirected graph should never have one at all — that mismatch is the bug, made impossible to miss.

5.question: Complete addUndirectedEdge so the connection is symmetric: g->adjacency[u][v] = 1; g->adjacency[___][___] = 1;
hints: The second line should set the reverse direction.
Swap the order of u and v from the first line.
5.solution: g->adjacency[v][u] = 1; — both directions must be set for a single undirected edge to be represented correctly.
